result.markdown: --- title: "Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Data Visualization" description: "Designing an infographic from the volunteer-collected \"What's in Season\" species data" date: 2026-10-13 categories: [R, Data Visualization] image: wildflower.jpeg citation: url: https://avarobillard.github.io/posts/wildflower-phenology bibliography: references.bib draft: false #draft-mode: linked --- ## Wildflower Watch: Years in Bloom #### Exploring the "What's in Season" data, collected by volunteers at the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Growing up in Texas, my grandmother used to take me to the Wildflower Center to watch the butterflies around the pollinator gardens as a child, and it was wonderful to be able to apply my education in plant science and data science to produce a visualization based around the same flowers and gardens. The University of Texas at Austin Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center is the Botanic Garden of Texas, with a mission to inspire the conservation and cultivation of native plants. The Wildflower Center was founded by Lady Bird Johnson and Helen Hayes as the National Wildflower Research Center in 1982 and later renamed the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center in 1997, and is a signature piece of Mrs. Johnson’s environmental legacy [@wildflowercenter]. The data I analyzed was sourced from the "What's in Season" tracker, a plant list of 1-24 species collected by approximately 20 volunteers at the Wildflower Center over a period of 15 years (2011 to present day). These plants were noted for being in bloom, growing, making seeds, or being otherwise noticeable. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Lady Bird Johnson- [@ladybirdday]](ladybird.jpg){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Image of Lady Bird Johnson perched on a rock' width=70%} ::: ::: Native plants provide a variety of benefits, including water conservation, providing habitat for birds, pollinators, and other wildlife, protecting soils, mitigating flooding, reducing mowing costs, and saving money on fertilizer and pesticides. These plants support balanced, hardy ecosystems and give us a sense of place. Using data from the "What's in Season" tracker, I created an infographic to address the following questions about the native plants observed by volunteers over the years at the Wildflower Center: - How many unique species were observed? - Have there been any shifts in phenology over time? - What were the most commonly observed species, overall and by month? - When did these species bloom throughout the year? You can explore the "What's in Season" tracker [here](https://www.wildflower.org/whatsinseason). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Infographic.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Full infographic exploring wildflower diveristy.' width=90%} ::: ::: Overall, my I found that many species were observed frequently with over 100 observations, such as Mealy blue sage, Rock rose, and Chocolate daisy. However, there was still a lot of variety in these observations, as 105 species were only noted once between 2011 and 2026. I designed heat maps exploring how the frequency of observations changed over the years for the top species, and did not notice any common pattern or shift in blooming times. Exploring the most commonly noted species in each month was very interesting, with Rock rose appearing throughout the summer months and Possumhaw in the winter. The Bluebonnet being the most commonly noted in March is no surprise, as this is the beginning of the peak blooming period for the beloved Texas state flower! Understanding the patterns in when native species are noticeable to people is very important for encouraging the adoption of native plants in gardens and landscapes, from keeping well-loved seasonal natives in stock at plant nurseries to providing more diverse options and encouraging the planting of species that are typically less noticed or common. My infographic is made up of three plots which were created using the {ggplot2} package in R and Affinity Designer. Let's explore some key pieces and the behind-the-scenes of my design choices! ## Overall design For my **font**, I selected **Rubik** for headings and titles and **Karla** for subtitles, axes, and captions. **Rubik** was a font I selected to closely match the branding used by the Wildflower Center, accessible through Google Fonts for use in R and Affinity. For my **color palette**, I color matched the green from the Wildflower Center website, and created a custom palette in R for each species I included. These colors were sourced using a color picker in my browser, [ColorZilla](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/colorzilla/bhlhnicpbhignbdhedgjhgdocnmhomnp), which allowed me to extract hex codes from images of the flower I was analyzing from the Wildflower Center plant images database. ## Plots I Always enjoy incorporating hand-drawn illustrations into my data visualizations, and was able to do so with the **Flowers of the year** plot. It was important to include these drawings to associate numbers and data with a recognizable flower. I used Goodnotes to sketch each flower, and exported the image into GIMP, another graphic design platform, to make the image background transparent. Finally, I imported each flower into Affinity and aligned them over each month. I later added the Zigzag Iris and Rock rose to the bar chart and heat map to create balance throughout the infographic. The full repository can be accessed on GitHub [here](https://github.com/avarobillard/wildflower-phenology). If you would like to explore the code used to make these plots, see below! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Import libraries library(tidyverse) library(here) library(ggplot2) library(plotly) library(showtext) library(ggtext) # Read in data bloom <- read_csv(here::here("data", "bloom_clean.csv")) ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## Establish fonts and colors ---- ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ # Add fonts font_add_google(name = "Rubik", family = "rubik") # Headings and titles font_add_google(name = "Karla", family = "karla") # Subtitles, axes, and captions showtext_auto() # Create color palette bloom_palette <- c("Wildflower center green" = "#60721C", "White" = "#F9FAFA", "floral1" = "#EA71D5", "floral2" = "#F0A0C6", "floral3" = "#5F7ECB") # Select species colors for plot- color matche from flower images species_colors <- c( "Turk's cap" = "#FA3B25", "Texas lantana" = "#F9740A", "Rock rose" = "#F865AE", "Purple coneflower" = "#E49CEC", "Prairie verbena" = "#7D7ADA", "Mealy blue sage" = "#5677EE", "Gregg's mistflower" = "#BDB7DB", "Chocolate daisy" = "#D9C703", "Bluebonnet" = "#0B67BF", "Autumn sage" = "#DE03B5" ) # Create list of common names to pull from as-needed common_names <- tribble( ~scientific_name, ~common_name, "Salvia farinacea", "Mealy blue sage", "Pavonia lasiopetala", "Rock rose", "Berlandiera lyrata", "Chocolate daisy", "Malvaviscus arboreus var. drummondii", "Turk's cap", "Conoclinium dissectum", "Gregg's mistflower", "Salvia greggii", "Autumn sage", "Echinacea purpurea", "Purple coneflower", "Lupinus texensis", "Bluebonnet", "Glandularia bipinnatifida", "Prairie verbena", "Lantana urticoides", "Texas lantana", "Ilex decidua", "Possumhaw", "Gelsemium sempervirens", "Carolina Jessamine", "Liatris punctata var. mucronata", "Texas blazing star", "Senna lindheimeriana", "Lindheimer's senna", "Helianthus maximiliani", "Maximilian sunflower", "Ilex vomitoria", "Yaupon holly", "Viguiera stenoloba", "Skeleton-leaf goldeneye" ) ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## Step 1: Collect statistics for use in header ---- ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## Total species count # How many unique species were observed over the full time period? # Count unique scientific names totalspecies <- bloom %>% summarise(unique_count = n_distinct(scientific_name)) #### Total observations # How many plants were listed total over the full time period? # Number of rows where scientific name is not NA nrow(bloom %>% filter(!is.na(scientific_name))) #### Number of plants observed once # Unique observations unique <- bloom %>% filter(!is.na(scientific_name)) %>% mutate(year = year(date)) %>% count(scientific_name) %>% filter(n == 1) %>% left_join(bloom %>% mutate(year = year(date)), by = "scientific_name") %>% select(scientific_name, year, n) nrow(unique) ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## Step 2: Bar plot of top species ---- ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## What were the top 10 most commonly noted plants over full time period? # Top 10 most commonly noted plants over full data top10 <- bloom %>% filter(!is.na(scientific_name)) %>% count(scientific_name) %>% slice_max(n, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) # Add common names for plotting top10 <- top10 %>% left_join(common_names, by = "scientific_name") # Create bar plot p1 <- ggplot(top10, aes(x = fct_reorder(common_name, n, .desc = TRUE), y = n, fill = common_name)) + geom_col(alpha = 0.75) + scale_fill_manual(values = species_colors, guide = "none") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme( plot.title = element_text(family = "rubik", face = "bold", size = rel(1.9), margin = margin(b = 6)), plot.subtitle = element_text(family = "karla", size = rel(1.2)), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1, size = 12.5, family = "karla"), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12.5, family = "karla")) p1 ggsave(here("figures", "top10bar.pdf"), width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 150, bg = "white", device = cairo_pdf) ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## Step 3: Phenology heatmap ---- ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## Are there any changing seasonal patterns in the most common species? # Filter data to top 4 most common species heatmap_data2 <- bloom %>% filter(scientific_name %in% c("Pavonia lasiopetala")) %>% mutate(year = year(date), month = month(date, label = TRUE)) %>% count(scientific_name, year, month) %>% complete(scientific_name, year, month, fill = list(n = 0)) # Create heatmap p2 <- ggplot(heatmap_data2, aes(x = month, y = year, fill = n)) + geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) + labs(fill = "Observation count", title = "**Rock rose** *(Pavonia lasiopetala)*") + scale_fill_gradientn(colors = c("#f5e1f0", "#F89BEA", "#FC47B0")) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(2012, 2026, by = 2)) + guides(fill = guide_colorbar(barwidth = 15, barheight = 0.75, title.position = "top")) + scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) + theme_minimal() + theme( legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_text(family = "karla", hjust = 0.5), axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(family = "karla"), plot.title = element_markdown(family = "rubik", size = rel(1.8), margin = margin(b = 6)), plot.subtitle = element_text(family = "karla", size = rel(1.2)), ) p2 ggsave(here("figures", "heatmap2.pdf"), width = 10, height = 10, dpi = 150, bg = "white") ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## Step 4: Bloom calendar heatmap ---- ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## When were the top 10 most common plants blooming throughout the year? # Count of observations of each species each month species_month_counts <- bloom %>% mutate(month = month(date, label = TRUE)) %>% count(scientific_name, month) # Fill all missing months with 0 species_month_counts <- species_month_counts %>% complete(scientific_name, month, fill = list(n = 0)) # Filter to just top 10 most common species species_month_counts <- species_month_counts %>% filter(scientific_name %in% top10$scientific_name) %>% left_join(common_names, by = "scientific_name") # Design heatmap with color edits species_month_counts <- species_month_counts %>% mutate(common_name = fct_reorder(common_name, n, .fun = sum, .desc = TRUE)) %>% group_by(common_name) %>% mutate( tile_color = { ramp <- colorRampPalette(c("#cfdb9a", species_colors[as.character(common_name[1])])) ramp(100)[as.integer(scales::rescale(n, to = c(1, 100)))] } ) %>% ungroup() ggplot(species_month_counts, aes(x = as.numeric(month), y = 1, fill = tile_color)) + geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) + scale_fill_identity() + facet_wrap(~common_name, ncol = 1, strip.position = "left") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb, expand = c(0, 0)) + theme_minimal() + theme( axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16, family = "karla"), axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1, size = 13, family = "karla"), panel.spacing = unit(0, "lines") ) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) ggsave(here("figures", "seasonalheatmap2.pdf"), width = 19, height = 6, dpi = 150) ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## Step 5: Plot of monthly plants ---- ##~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ ## What were the most commonly observed plants in each month of the year? # Most observed plants each month (2011-2026) top_by_month <- bloom %>% filter(!is.na(scientific_name)) %>% mutate(month = month(date, label = TRUE)) %>% count(month, scientific_name) %>% group_by(month) %>% slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) %>% ungroup() top_by_month <- top_by_month %>% left_join(common_names, by = "scientific_name") ``` :::
